result: Two unrelated patients with lipoatrophic diabetes were identified carrying de novo pathogenic variants in EPHX1 (p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg), which are absent from population databases, affect highly conserved amino acids, and are predicted pathogenic by multiple algorithms.
evaluation: Claims C3, C28, C49, C50, C53, C56, C57, and C60 collectively demonstrate the identification of two de novo EPHX1 variants through WES and Sanger sequencing (Figure 1), confirmed by segregation analysis, with strong in silico evidence of pathogenicity. The variants are absent from gnomAD and affect evolutionarily conserved residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

result: The identified EPHX1 variants are localized in the catalytic domain near critical residues of the catalytic triad (Asp226, Glu404, His431), strongly suggesting they affect enzyme activity.
evaluation: Claims C45, C46, C119, C122, C124, and C125 are supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2B-C. The variants p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg are positioned in close proximity to the catalytic triad residues, providing structural evidence for their predicted pathogenic effect.

result: The p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg variants led to near-complete loss of EPHX1 hydrolysis activity in c-SO assays, while control variants (p.Tyr113His, p.His139Arg, p.Glu404Asp) retained activity, demonstrating specific functional impairment.
evaluation: Claims C126-C132 are strongly supported by enzyme activity assays shown in Figure 2D-E. The patient variants show near-complete loss of c-SO hydrolysis activity compared to wild-type and control variants, with protein expression levels remaining largely unchanged (except slight reduction for p.Gly430Arg), indicating the effect is due to loss of catalytic function rather than protein instability.

result: The p.Thr333Pro and p.Gly430Arg variants cause EPHX1 protein aggregation within the endoplasmic reticulum, forming higher-order complexes not observed with wild-type or other mutant isoforms.
evaluation: Claims C4, C136-C141 are supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 3A-B) and western blot/immunoprecipitation data (Figure 3C). The patient variants show distinct clumping within the ER and formation of oligomers (~150 kDa) in addition to monomers (~55 kDa), which is not observed with wild-type or control variants. The aggregation persists even when the Flag tag is removed, ruling out tag-related artifacts.

result: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Ephx1 knockout in 3T3-L1 pre-adipocytes abolished adipocyte differentiation, as evidenced by reduced lipid droplet formation and decreased expression of adipogenic markers (PPARγ, C/EBPα, SREBP-1c, FAS, adiponectin).
evaluation: Claims C6, C143-C147, and C150 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: western blot confirmation of Ephx1 loss (Figure 4B), enzyme activity assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), Oil Red O staining showing dramatic reduction in lipid droplets (Figure 4C-D, p<0.0001), and western blot showing reduced adipogenic markers (Figure 4E). The phenotype was replicated with a second gRNA targeting a different exon (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), ruling out off-target effects.

result: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Ephx1 knockout decreased insulin response in both pre-adipocytes and differentiated adipocytes, as shown by reduced phosphorylation of insulin signaling intermediates (IRβ, IRS1, AKT, ERK) upon insulin stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C7, C148, and C149 are supported by western blot data in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4. Wild-type and control cells show robust phosphorylation of insulin signaling intermediates upon insulin stimulation, while Ephx1 KO cells show markedly reduced or absent phosphorylation, demonstrating insulin resistance at the cellular level.

result: Ephx1 knockout in 3T3-L1 pre-adipocytes promoted oxidative stress, with significantly higher ROS levels compared to wild-type and control cells (p<0.0001).
evaluation: Claims C8, C156, and C179 are supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 5A. The Ephx1 KO cells display significantly elevated ROS levels compared to both wild-type and control cells, with statistical significance (p<0.0001).

result: Ephx1 knockout promoted cellular senescence in both 3T3-L1 pre-adipocytes and human ASCs, as evidenced by reduced BrdU incorporation, increased P21/P16/phospho-P53 levels, and markedly increased SA-β-gal activity (p<0.0001 in 3T3-L1, p<0.001 in ASCs).
evaluation: Claims C9, C157-C163 are supported by multiple senescence markers across two cell types. In 3T3-L1 cells: reduced BrdU incorporation (Figure 5B), increased P21/P16/phospho-P53 (Figure 5C), and increased SA-β-gal activity (Figure 5D-E). In human ASCs: increased phospho-P53/P21/P16 (Figure 5F) and ~20-fold increase in SA-β-gal activity (Figure 5G-H). The consistency across cell types and multiple markers strongly supports the senescence phenotype.

result: Patient 1-derived fibroblasts confirmed oxidative stress and cellular senescence ex vivo, showing increased ROS (p<0.0001), altered morphology, reduced BrdU incorporation (p<0.0001), increased P21/P16/phospho-P53, and markedly increased SA-β-gal activity (p<0.0001).
evaluation: Claims C10, C166-C171 are supported by data from patient-derived fibroblasts (Figure 6). The patient fibroblasts show increased ROS (Figure 6A), altered morphology (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), reduced proliferation (Figure 6B), increased senescence markers (Figure 6C), and increased SA-β-gal activity (Figure 6D-E). These findings parallel the results from Ephx1 KO cell models, providing ex vivo validation of the cellular phenotypes.

result: Metreleptin therapy had beneficial effects in patient 1, leading to decreased HbA1c (from 11.6-16.5% to 7.3% after 6 months), ~50% reduction in insulin requirements, and improvement in liver enzymes and liver scores.
evaluation: Claims C11, C195-C198 are supported by clinical data presented in Table 2. The patient showed substantial improvement in multiple metabolic parameters after metreleptin treatment, including glycemic control (HbA1c decreased to 7.3%), reduced insulin requirements (from 15 IU/kg/day to ~7.5 IU/kg/day), and improved liver function markers. This represents a clinically meaningful therapeutic response.

result: Patient 1 presented with a complex multisystemic phenotype including microcephaly, dysmorphic features, progressive lipoatrophy (total fat mass 15.8%, Z-score -2.8), severe insulin-resistant diabetes (HbA1c 18.9% at diagnosis), hepatomegaly with liver steatosis, hyperandrogenism, neurological manifestations (intellectual disability, axonal neuropathy), and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
evaluation: Claims C47, C61-C95 provide comprehensive clinical characterization of patient 1 supported by clinical examination, laboratory measurements, DXA scans (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), imaging (Figure 1D), and photographs (Figure 1C-G). The data are internally consistent and presented in Table 1. The multisystemic nature of the phenotype is well-documented across multiple organ systems.

result: Patient 2 presented with similar features to patient 1, including dysmorphic features, lipoatrophy (total fat mass 12.4%, first percentile), insulin resistance (fasting insulin 284 pmol/L), severe hypertriglyceridemia (21.9 mmol/L), elevated liver enzymes, and profound sensorineural hearing loss since birth.
evaluation: Claims C52, C96-C111 provide clinical characterization of patient 2 supported by clinical examination, laboratory measurements, and DXA scans (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The data are presented in Table 1. While patient 2 shares core features with patient 1 (lipoatrophy, insulin resistance, liver dysfunction, hearing loss), there are differences in severity and specific manifestations (e.g., not diabetic at last investigation, more severe hypertriglyceridemia).

result: The two patients share multiple clinical features including dysmorphic features, lipoatrophy, insulin resistance, hypertriglyceridemia, liver dysfunction, and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, establishing a consistent phenotype associated with EPHX1 variants.
evaluation: Claims C112 and C205 are supported by the clinical data from both patients presented in Table 1 and throughout the Results section. The overlap in clinical features between two unrelated patients with different de novo variants in the same gene provides strong evidence for a consistent disease phenotype, though with some variability in severity and specific manifestations.

result: Patient 1's plasma showed accumulation of 7,8 epoxydocosapentaenoic acid and decreased corresponding diol (7,8 dihydroxydocosapentaenoic acid), consistent with impaired EPHX1 function.
evaluation: Claims C133 and C134 are supported by LC-MS/MS data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing altered EpFA/diol ratios in patient 1 compared to controls. However, the authors acknowledge that oxylipin profiling is an emerging field with difficult biological interpretation, and they note that further experiments in additional patients or cellular models are needed to confirm this observation. The finding is consistent with loss of EPHX1 function but requires additional validation.

result: The pathogenic effect of the EPHX1 variants may involve a dominant negative mechanism, suggested by protein aggregation and potential dimeric structure, though co-expression experiments did not detect dominant negative effects in enzyme activity assays.
evaluation: Claims C142, C173-C178 present speculation about a dominant negative mechanism based on: (1) presence of loss-of-function variants in gnomAD (C172), (2) protein aggregation data (Figure 3), and (3) literature suggesting EPHX1 may be dimeric (C174). However, co-expression experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) did not show dominant negative effects, and the authors acknowledge overexpression studies may not be appropriate for testing this hypothesis (C177). The final result is loss of enzyme activity (C178), but the mechanism (haploinsufficiency vs. dominant negative) remains uncertain.

result: This study presents the first example of pathogenic variants in an epoxide hydrolase gene (EPHX1) causing monogenic disease in humans, which can be classified as 'pathogenic' according to ACMG criteria with functional data.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C12, C13, C27, C201, and C204 establish the novelty of this finding. The statement that no pathogenic variants in EH genes had been reported prior to this study (C2, C27) is supported by the literature review. The ACMG classification as 'pathogenic' (C204) is justified by the combination of genetic evidence (de novo occurrence, absence from population databases, conservation, in silico predictions) and functional data (loss of enzyme activity, protein aggregation, cellular phenotypes).

result: EPHX1 is widely expressed with highest expression in liver, adipose tissue, and adrenal glands, is evolutionarily conserved, and is retained in ER microsomal membranes, explaining how germline variants result in a multisystemic phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C33, C35, C36, C114, C115, C135, and C206 are supported by citations to previous literature and conservation data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The broad expression pattern and evolutionary conservation are well-established, and the inference that this explains the multisystemic phenotype (C206) is reasonable given the clinical data from both patients.

result: Ephx1 knockout mice showed no obvious phenotype, but differences between human and mouse lipid metabolism, the autosomal recessive nature of most CGL models, and the potential dominant negative effect of these variants suggest knock-in mice with additional metabolic stress may be needed to model the human phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C185-C192 are supported by citations to previous literature. The authors appropriately discuss the limitations of existing Ephx1 knockout mice (C185-C186) and provide context about differences between mouse models of CGL vs. partial lipodystrophy (C187-C190). The suggestion that knock-in mice with metabolic stress may be needed (C191-C192) is a reasonable inference based on the cited literature and the nature of the variants.

result: Drugs metabolized by EPHX1 (carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin) are contraindicated for patients with EPHX1 deficiency due to risk of toxicity from impaired metabolism.
evaluation: Claims C199 and C200 represent a clinical recommendation based on EPHX1's established role in xenobiotic metabolism (supported by citation C199) and the demonstrated loss of enzyme activity in the patients. While C200 is speculation about consequences, it is reasonable speculation based on established pharmacology. This is an important practical implication for patient care.

result: Despite extensive research, the full spectrum of epoxide hydrolase substrates and biological functions in humans remain partly unknown, and it is challenging to define the contribution of each EH in human disorders, though association studies suggest pleiotropic roles.
evaluation: Claims C23-C26 are supported by citation to a review article (C23) and citations to association studies (C25). These claims provide appropriate context about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study. The inference about pleiotropic roles (C26) is reasonable based on the association study data.
